user_query: My employer hasn't paid my salary for 3 months. What can I do?
variations: Boss owes me salary. Where do I report?
How do I claim unpaid wages?
Company never pay me three months already
Who do I complain to if I don't get paid?
part_a_general_info: Under the Employment Act 1968, employers must pay salary within 7 days after the end of each salary period. If unpaid, you may file a salary claim with the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM). Claims must generally be filed within 1 year from the date salary was due; if you have left the company, within 6 months of your last day. The Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT) can hear claims up to $20,000 ($30,000 with union assistance). Mediation at TADM is mandatory before ECT.
triage_questions: Are you still working for the employer, or have you left?
When was the last salary payment you received?
How much salary is owed in total?
Are you a Singapore Citizen, PR, or on a work permit?
Have you already filed a claim with TADM?
branching_logic: If Q1 = left → Check if within 6-month limitation; if outside, flag as time-barred and escalate.
If Q4 = work permit → Additionally inform about MOM regulations.
If Q5 = already filed TADM → Branch to ECT pathway.
routing: Route A (No TADM claim): Refer to TADM for mandatory mediation. Provide filing link and limitation period.
Route B (TADM failed): If Claim Referral Certificate obtained, refer to ECT; refer to PBSG employment clinic if needed.
Route C (Work permit holder): Additionally refer to MOM. Escalate to PBSG staff for specialist referral.
Route D (Time-barred): Inform claim may be time-barred. Escalate to PBSG staff to assess exceptions.
guardrail: Must NOT advise on specific contractual entitlements or draft any letter of demand. General statutory framework and routing only.

user_query: I was fired unfairly. What can I do?
variations: My boss sacked me for no reason
I got terminated without warning
Is it legal for my company to fire me like this?
I was dismissed and I think it's wrongful
part_a_general_info: Wrongful dismissal under the Employment Act 1968 means dismissal without just cause or excuse (e.g. discriminatory grounds, to deprive benefits, or for exercising employment rights). Claims must be filed with TADM within 1 month of dismissal. If mediation fails, the matter is referred to the ECT. If the employer gave notice or salary in lieu per contract, it may be lawful termination even if felt unfair.
triage_questions: When were you dismissed? (1-month limitation)
Were you given a reason?
Were you given notice or salary in lieu?
Do you believe it was on discriminatory grounds or to deprive you of a benefit?
Have you already filed with TADM?
branching_logic: If Q1 = more than 1 month ago → Flag as potentially time-barred. Escalate urgently.
If Q3 = yes, received notice → Focus shifts to whether underlying reason was discriminatory or retaliatory.
If Q4 = discrimination identified → Additionally inform about TAFEP.
routing: Route A (Within 1 month, no TADM): Refer to TADM urgently. Emphasize limitation period.
Route B (Discrimination element): Refer to TADM and TAFEP; if union member, refer to union.
Route C (TADM failed): Refer to ECT; if above $20,000, refer to PBSG clinic for civil court.
Route D (Time-barred): Escalate to PBSG staff to assess if exceptions apply.
guardrail: Must NOT assess whether dismissal constitutes 'just cause or excuse'. General framework and routing only.

user_query: I'm a freelancer and my client won't pay me. Can I go to TADM?
variations: I do delivery and they owe me money
My contract work client hasn't paid
I'm self-employed, can I claim salary?
Platform company owes me payment
part_a_general_info: The Employment Act generally covers employees under a contract of service. Freelancers under a contract for service are generally not covered and cannot use TADM or ECT. Platform workers who are members of a platform work association may access specific channels under the Platform Workers Act 2024. For non-payment, freelancers can use the Small Claims Tribunal (up to $20,000) or Magistrate's Court (up to $60,000). Sending a Letter of Demand and trying mediation at the CMC is advisable before filing.
triage_questions: Describe your working arrangement — do you set your own hours?
Do you have a written contract? Is it a 'contract of service' or 'contract for service'?
Are you a platform worker and member of a platform work association?
How much is the outstanding amount?
branching_logic: If Q1 suggests employer-employee relationship despite 'freelancer' label → Escalate to PBSG staff for assessment.
If Q3 = platform worker with association → Route to association.
If Q4 ≤ $20,000 → SCT; if $20k–$60k → Magistrate's Court.
routing: Route A (Freelancer, ≤$20k): Refer to SCT. Advise Letter of Demand first.
Route B (Freelancer, >$20k): Refer to Magistrate's/District Court. Refer to PBSG civil law clinic.
Route C (Possibly misclassified): Escalate to PBSG staff for employee/freelancer assessment.
Route D (Platform worker): Refer to platform work association.
guardrail: Must NOT determine whether applicant is an employee or freelancer. Identify indicators and escalate.

user_query: I was injured at work. My boss won't pay medical bills.
variations: Got hurt at workplace, employer refuses to pay
Work accident — who pays?
I fell at the construction site, what are my rights?
Boss says injury is my fault, won't cover medical
part_a_general_info: Under the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA), employers must compensate employees for work-related injuries regardless of fault. This covers medical leave wages and medical expenses. The injury should be reported to MOM by filing a work injury report. Employers must report injuries resulting in more than 3 days of medical leave. WICA claims must generally be filed within 1 year of the accident or within 1 year of diagnosis for occupational diseases. WICA is a no-fault scheme; negligence need not be proven. If the injury was caused by employer negligence, a common law claim for damages may also be possible, but both WICA and common law cannot be pursued for the same injury.
triage_questions: When and where did the injury occur?
What injuries did you suffer? Did you receive medical attention?
Has your employer filed an incident report with MOM?
How long have you been on medical leave?
Are you a Singapore Citizen/PR or a foreign worker?
branching_logic: If Q3 = employer has not reported → Inform applicant they can file directly with MOM.
If Q5 = foreign worker → Additional protections may apply; check work permit status.
If serious/permanent injury → Applicant may wish to consider common law claim (requires legal advice).
routing: Route A (Standard WICA claim): Refer to MOM for WICA claim filing. Provide online filing link.
Route B (Employer not cooperating): Advise applicant to file incident report with MOM directly. Refer to PBSG employment clinic.
Route C (Foreign worker): Refer to Migrant Workers' Centre and/or PBSG Migrant Workers' Law Centre.
Route D (Serious/permanent injury): Escalate to PBSG staff. Applicant may need legal advice on WICA vs common law claim.
guardrail: Must NOT advise on whether to pursue WICA or common law, nor assess liability. General framework only.

user_query: My company didn't pay my CPF.
variations: Employer not contributing CPF
Boss never top up my CPF
How to check if CPF was paid by employer?
Company owes me CPF contributions
part_a_general_info: Under the Central Provident Fund Act 1953, employers are required to make CPF contributions for Singapore Citizens or Permanent Residents. Non-payment of CPF is a criminal offence. Applicants can check their CPF contributions via the CPF website or app. If non-payment is confirmed, they can lodge a report with the CPF Board. The CPF Board has enforcement powers to recover arrears and can prosecute employers who fail to pay (fines or imprisonment).
triage_questions: How long has your employer not been contributing CPF?
Have you checked your CPF statement to confirm non-payment?
Are you a Singapore Citizen or PR?
Are you still employed with this company?
branching_logic: If Q3 = not SC/PR → CPF contributions are generally not required for non-residents. Different issue.
If Q4 = still employed → Advise caution; approach may affect employment relationship.
routing: Route A (Confirmed non-payment, SC/PR): Refer to CPF Board to lodge a report; CPF Board will investigate and enforce.
Route B (Non-resident): Inform that CPF is generally not required for non-residents. If salary dispute, refer to TADM instead.
Route C (Left employment): Refer to CPF Board and concurrently to TADM if there are other outstanding salary claims.
guardrail: Must NOT advise on specific CPF contribution amounts or calculate arrears. Refer to CPF Board.

user_query: My boss refuses to pay me for overtime work.
variations: I worked extra hours but got no money
Is OT pay mandatory?
Company says no overtime pay for my role
Claiming money for working weekends and public holidays
part_a_general_info: Under Part 4 of the Employment Act 1968, overtime (OT) pay is mandatory only for: (a) workmen (manual labour) earning up to $4,500/month, and (b) non-workmen earning up to $2,600/month. For these employees, OT must be paid at 1.5 times the hourly basic rate of pay. Managers and executives are generally not covered under Part 4; their entitlement to OT depends strictly on their employment contract.
triage_questions: What is your job role (e.g. manual worker, clerk, manager)?
What is your basic monthly salary?
Does your employment contract specifically mention overtime pay?
Are you a Singapore Citizen/PR or Work Permit holder?
branching_logic: If Q1 = Manager OR Q2 > $2,600 (non-workman) → Statutory OT likely does not apply; depends on contract.
If Q4 = Work Permit → Route to MOM/TADM with language support if needed.
routing: Route A (Covered under Part 4): File claim at TADM.
Route B (Not covered, contract silent): Statutory claim unlikely to succeed. Refer to PBSG Employment Clinic for contract review if amount substantial.
Route C (Not covered, contract provides OT): File claim at TADM for breach of contract.
guardrail: Must NOT calculate the specific OT sum owed or interpret ambiguous contract clauses.
